name: Achilles
summary: Son of the mortal king Peleus and the sea-nymph Thetis, Achilles leads the Myrmidons. His rage at Agamemnon — the very first word of the poem in Greek — drives the whole story.

moments.text: Agamemnon takes his prize, Briseis. Achilles withdraws from the fighting and asks Thetis to make the Greeks regret it.
Refuses Agamemnon's lavish offer of gifts, even with Briseis returned.
Learns Patroclus is dead and turns his rage against Hector.
Kills Hector and drags his body behind his chariot.
Weeps with Priam and gives back Hector's body.

fate: His death is foretold — Hector, dying, names Paris and Apollo as his killers — but it happens after the poem ends.
fact: The famous 'Achilles heel' never appears in the Iliad. In Book 21 a spear from Asteropaeus grazes his arm and draws blood.

name: Agamemnon
role: King of Mycenae, commander of the Greeks
summary: Elder brother of Menelaus and leader of the whole Greek army. His pride sparks the quarrel that nearly loses the war.

moments.text: Forced to return Chryseis to end Apollo's plague, he takes Briseis from Achilles.
Tests the army by suggesting they sail home — and they nearly do.
Admits his mistake and sends an embassy with gifts to Achilles.
Publicly reconciles with Achilles and returns Briseis.

fate: Survives the war. His murder on returning home is told in the Odyssey, not the Iliad.
fact: When he finally apologises in Book 19, he blames Ate — the goddess of ruinous folly — for clouding his mind.

name: Menelaus
summary: The war began over his wife Helen, who left Sparta with Paris. He fights hard to win her back and to defend his friends.

moments.text: Fights Paris in a duel for Helen and is about to win when Aphrodite whisks Paris away.
Wounded by an arrow from Pandarus, breaking the truce.
Defends the body of Patroclus against the Trojans.

fate: Survives the war; the Odyssey shows him home in Sparta with Helen.
fact: In the duel he grabs Paris by the horsehair crest of his helmet and starts dragging him toward the Greeks.

image.title: Menelaus Supporting the Body of Patroclus

name: Odysseus
summary: The cleverest of the Greeks, valued for his speeches and cool head as much as his spear.

moments.text: Stops the army from fleeing to the ships and silences the troublemaker Thersites.
Gives the main speech in the embassy to Achilles.
Goes on a night raid with Diomedes behind Trojan lines.

fate: Survives. His ten-year journey home is the subject of the Odyssey.
fact: The Wooden Horse — Odysseus's most famous trick — is not in the Iliad at all.

image.title: Ulysses and Diomedes in the Tent of Rhesus (detail)

name: Ajax
role: Son of Telamon, the Greeks' great defender
summary: Huge, steady and nearly unstoppable, Ajax is the best Greek fighter while Achilles sulks. His great shield protects the army.

moments.text: Duels Hector until nightfall; they part as equals and swap gifts.
Joins the embassy to Achilles.
Defends the Greek ships almost single-handedly.

fate: Survives the poem. His later fate is told by other poets, not Homer's Iliad.
fact: After their duel Hector gives Ajax a silver-studded sword, and Ajax gives Hector a purple belt.

name: Patroclus
summary: Gentle and loyal, Patroclus cannot bear to watch the Greeks die. He borrows Achilles' armour to save the ships — and pays with his life.

moments.text: Tends the wounded and hears Nestor's plea to bring Achilles back.
Wears Achilles' armour, drives the Trojans back and kills Sarpedon.
Is struck by Apollo, wounded by Euphorbus and killed by Hector.

fate: Dies in Book 16. His funeral and games fill Book 23.
fact: Achilles warned him to stop once the ships were safe. Patroclus pushed on toward Troy instead.

name: Hector
summary: Eldest son of Priam and Hecuba, Hector carries Troy's defence on his shoulders. A loving husband and father who fights for his city knowing it may fall.

moments.text: Says farewell to his wife Andromache and baby son on the walls.
Smashes the gate of the Greek wall with a boulder.
Kills Patroclus, who is wearing Achilles' armour.
Faces Achilles alone outside the walls and is killed.

fate: Killed by Achilles in Book 22. The poem's last line describes his funeral.
fact: His baby son is frightened by Hector's nodding helmet crest — so Hector takes it off to hold him.

name: Priam
summary: Father of Hector and Paris, Priam watches his sons die one by one. His night journey to Achilles is the emotional heart of the final book.

moments.text: Kindly asks Helen to name the Greek heroes from the walls.
Begs Hector from the walls not to face Achilles.
Crosses enemy lines at night to ransom Hector's body.

fate: Alive when the poem ends. Troy's fall comes later, in other poems.
fact: Priam tells Achilles he had fifty sons when the Greeks arrived — nineteen of them from one mother.

image.title: Priam Asks Achilles to Return Hector's Body

name: Paris
summary: Handsome and favoured by Aphrodite, Paris brought Helen to Troy and started the war. He is a skilled archer but often avoids the front line.

moments.text: Challenges Menelaus to a duel, loses, and is rescued by Aphrodite.
Hector finds him at home and shames him back to battle.
Wounds Diomedes in the foot with an arrow.

fate: Survives the poem. Hector's dying words predict Paris and Apollo will kill Achilles.
fact: The 'Judgment of Paris' is only hinted at in the Iliad, in Book 24.

name: Helen
role: Queen of Sparta living in Troy
summary: Wife of Menelaus, she left Sparta with Paris. In Troy she is surrounded by a war fought over her, and often blames herself.

moments.text: Names the Greek heroes for Priam from the walls of Troy.
Tells Hector she wishes she had died before the war began.
Mourns Hector as the one Trojan who was always kind to her.

fate: Alive at the end. The Odyssey shows her back in Sparta with Menelaus.
fact: At Hector's funeral three women lament him: Andromache, his mother Hecuba, and finally Helen.

image.title: Helen on the Walls of Troy

name: Andromache
summary: Daughter of Eetion of Thebe, Andromache has already lost her father and brothers to Achilles. Hector is now her whole family.

moments.text: Begs Hector to defend Troy from the walls instead of the open plain.
Hears the wailing, runs to the walls and sees Hector's body dragged away.
Leads the laments at Hector's funeral.

fate: Alive when the poem ends, fearing slavery for herself and her son.
fact: She tells Hector that Achilles killed her father and all seven of her brothers.
